findings.title: The name as an act of invocation
findings.claim: At the focus's word for name, wider passages make the formula legible as an invocation: they command calling God by His names, and one repeats the full basmala within a statement attributed to Sulayman.
findings.mechanism: The focus noun ism is bound to Allah in the opening formula. In 7:180 and 17:110, Allah's names are explicitly ways to call upon Him; in 27:30 the same complete formula introduces a statement from Sulayman. These independent uses meet the focus's name with invocation and framed speech, so bi-smi reads as an enacted address rather than a detached label.
findings.reader_payoff: The opening can be heard as calling upon God through His name, an act that frames what follows rather than a caption placed beside it.
findings.containment: The ordinary reading, in the name of Allah, the Merciful, the Compassionate, remains intact. These wider uses support an invocation function; they do not make the focus a direct vocative or prove that every basmala has the same pragmatic purpose.

epistemic.reason: The focus carrier and the target wording are supplied directly, but applying the wider invocation uses to this prefatory formula is a contextual inference; target morphology is not supplied.

branch_activations.branch_gloss: ad, adlandırma ve ad ya da nitelik bakımından denklik
branch_activations.facet_statement: Ad, bir varlığı tanıtan ve ondan söz etmeyi sağlayan söz veya anlamdır.
branch_activations.carrier: The focus stem ism carries the ordinary sense of a name or designation in bi-smi.
branch_activations.independent_trigger: 7:180 says to call upon God by His beautiful names; 17:110 directs calling Allah or al-Rahman; 27:30 places the full focus formula inside a statement attributed to Sulayman.
branch_activations.activation: The separate passages use divine names as means of invocation and place the same formula at the start of attributed speech. Their contact with the focus's ism changes the phrase from naming alone into an invocation that frames an utterance.
branch_activations.resulting_reading: The basmala is heard as an act of invoking God by name, not merely a label for God.
branch_activations.boundary: This contextual use does not change the focus's ordinary name sense, make its syntax a direct call, or establish that the cited passages are all making the same claim.

findings.title: The named Lord as the unshared object of worship
findings.claim: The focus's name for Allah meets wider statements that join worship of the Lord to the question of whether He has any namesake, and that contrast Him with human-assigned worship-names; the opening can therefore carry an orientation toward the unique, worshipped Lord.
findings.mechanism: The focus supplies both ism, name, and Allah, the named referent. In 19:65, the command to worship the Lord is followed by a question about whether He has a namesake; 12:40 contrasts humanly assigned names with rule and worship belonging only to Allah. The contact makes the focus's named referent more than a designation: it becomes the unshared direction of devotion.
findings.reader_payoff: In the opening formula, the name points toward one Lord without a namesake, and the invocation gains a devotional direction without replacing its plain wording.
findings.containment: The focus itself does not command worship or discuss invented names; those relations enter from the wider verses. The 12:40 reciprocal record also carries a no-value counter-reading that the focus's name alone does not clarify that verse, so this remains a bounded contextual echo rather than a direct allusion or lexical derivation.

epistemic.reason: The focus carriers and wider Arabic texts are supplied, but the relation is inferred across contexts. The 12:40 connection includes a reciprocal no-value counter-reading, and target morphology is unavailable.

branch_activations.independent_trigger: 19:65 asks whether the Lord has a namesake after commanding worship of Him; 12:40 speaks of names assigned by people and contrasts them with Allah's sole rule and worship.
branch_activations.activation: The namesake question and the contrast with human-assigned names meet the focus's name and its named referent, making uniqueness salient in the act of naming.
branch_activations.resulting_reading: The focus's name is heard as identifying an unshared divine referent rather than a name among humanly assigned alternatives.
branch_activations.boundary: The name remains an ordinary designation here; the wider contrast does not turn ism into a command or prove a direct allusion.

findings.title: Mercy as active care across creation and return
findings.claim: The two focus epithets name divine mercy; wider passages place that mercy in a created order without disparity, as a commitment alongside resurrection and punishment, and as a relation that calls for following. Together they let the pair read as active care with a cosmic and accountable reach.
findings.mechanism: The focus carries mercy twice through al-Rahman and al-Rahim. In 67:3, creation is attributed to al-Rahman and described as without disparity; 6:12 places mercy written upon God alongside gathering on the Day of Resurrection; 7:156 says mercy encompasses all things while distinguishing punishment; 20:90 names al-Rahman immediately before a call to follow and obey. These independent contexts make the focus's mercy a sustaining and governing relation, rather than a description detached from action.
findings.reader_payoff: The doubled mercy can be perceived as a force that sustains created life and remains present when return, judgment, and response come into view.
findings.containment: The focus still names God as merciful. The wider verses do not mean that 91:0 itself announces judgment or commands obedience, and they do not make mercy cancel punishment; they supply contextual reach without displacing the plain epithet pair.

epistemic.reason: The focus branch is accepted and the wider target Arabic is explicit, but the proposed relation among creation, mercy, judgment, and obedience is an interpretation across ayat; target morphology is not supplied.

branch_activations.facet_statement: Bu iç yöneliş, acınan kişiyi esirgemeyi ve ona iyilikte bulunmayı gerektiren etkin bir sonuç taşır.
branch_activations.carrier: The focus repeats the divine mercy sense in al-Rahman and al-Rahim.
branch_activations.independent_trigger: 6:12 says mercy is written upon God before gathering people to resurrection; 7:156 says His mercy encompasses all things while also naming punishment.
branch_activations.activation: These wider statements place mercy in sustained divine action and beside accountability, so the two focus epithets gain an active reach across a judgment horizon.
branch_activations.resulting_reading: The focus names mercy as an ongoing relation of care that remains present across return and accountability.
branch_activations.boundary: The target verses do not make the focus itself a statement about the Day of Judgment, and the relation does not imply that mercy cancels punishment.

branch_activations.facet_statement: Tanrı hakkında kullanıldığında esirgemenin genişliği ve yaratılmışlara iyilik olarak ulaşması belirginleşir.
branch_activations.carrier: The focus applies the mercy pair to God through al-Rahman and al-Rahim.
branch_activations.independent_trigger: 67:3 places al-Rahman in a creation without disparity; 7:156 says mercy encompasses all things; 20:90 names al-Rahman before a call to follow and obey.
branch_activations.activation: The wider contexts attach the same divine mercy designation to created order, broad reach, and a call for response; the focus's repeated epithets therefore carry more than an affective quality.
branch_activations.resulting_reading: The mercy named at the opening can be perceived as active beneficence that sustains creation and has a governing, relational reach.
branch_activations.boundary: These are wider contextual uses, not separate dictionary meanings forced into the focus; the target verses do not establish a complete system or make obedience a lexical component of mercy.
